statement: Whether "Homo habilis" represents one coherent species or should be split into Homo habilis sensu stricto and a separate species Homo rudolfensis remains an open, actively contested question in current paleoanthropology, not settled by consensus.
scholarly_disagreement: Whether early-Homo variability in East Africa (OH 7, OH 13, KNM-ER 1470, KNM-ER 1813, etc.) represents one variable species or at least two co-existing species.

sources.citation: Wood, B. Koobi Fora Research Project monograph proposing the habilis/rudolfensis split.
sources.author: Wood, B.

sources.citation: Spoor, F., Gunz, P., Neubauer, S., et al. "Reconstructed Homo habilis type OH 7 suggests deep-rooted species diversity in early Homo." Nature 519: 83-86.
sources.author: Spoor et al.

interpretations.position: Early Homo material should be split into H. habilis sensu stricto and H. rudolfensis
interpretations.strongest_case: Digital reconstruction of the crushed OH 7 mandible shows a long, narrow, primitive dental arcade distinct from other habilis-attributed material (e.g. OH 13, KNM-ER 1813), supporting real morphological diversity within "early Homo."

interpretations.position: The traditional single, variable Homo habilis taxon remains defensible

holders.name: Traditional Leakey/Tobias/Napier-descended position, surveyed without full resolution by Susan Antón
holders.work: "Early Homo: Who, When, and Where," Current Anthropology (2003, 2012 pieces)

interpretations.strongest_case: Variation among the attributed specimens falls within a plausible range for a single geographically and temporally dispersed species, given known intraspecific variability in other hominins.
